title: Collective search-and-capture under competing assignment policies
abstract: We study a minimal lattice model of active search-and-capture in which persistent random walkers locate and irreversibly capture immobile targets through a finite-range, mutually exclusive assignment rule. We measure the collective completion time $T_c$ as a function of the walkers' reorientation rate $α$ and the search radius $R$. The dependence $T_c(α)$ is non-monotonic, with a minimum at intermediate persistence whose depth decreases as $R$ grows. Capture kinetics show that $T_c$ is not a typical capture time but is governed by the extreme, late-time tail of the capture process, while the bulk of targets are captured much earlier; this tail is controlled mainly by the free-exploration phase rather than by the final directed approach. We then compare the baseline single-round assignment rule with cascading reassignment and with maximum-cardinality matching on a candidate graph. The two greedy policies (single-round and cascading) agree at very small $R$, whereas maximum-cardinality matching already produces a strong speedup at moderate $R$: improved matching reduces $T_c$ by factors of several at large $R$, and by more than an order of magnitude at moderate $R$. Thus, in this collective, depletion-coupled search problem, the assignment policy can control the capture time more strongly than the walkers' persistence.
summary: This paper analyzes a lattice model of active search-and-capture where mobile walkers compete for immobile targets. The core finding is that optimizing the assignment policy—specifically using maximum-cardinality matching—is a more powerful control parameter for reducing capture time than adjusting walker movement persistence. This highlights how coordination in resource allocation dictates the system's extreme-time behavior.
main_problem: The study investigates collective search-and-capture dynamics on a lattice, focusing on how different assignment policies affect the overall completion time ($T_c$).
main_result: The assignment policy can control $T_c$ more strongly than walker persistence ($\alpha$), with maximum-cardinality matching providing significant speedups over greedy approaches.
method: The authors use a minimal lattice model simulation approach, comparing baseline single-round assignment against cascading reassignment and maximum-cardinality matching algorithms.
model_or_system: The system is a minimal lattice model on a periodic square lattice containing mobile walkers and immobile targets. Capture occurs via an irreversible, finite-range, mutually exclusive assignment rule.
key_observables: Completion Time ($T_c$), $T_{50\%}$, $T_{90\%}$, and the instantaneous fraction of assigned walkers ($f_{	ext{assigned}}(t)$).
important_parameters: Walkers' reorientation rate ($\alpha$) and search radius ($R$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on extreme-value statistics, where $T_c$ is governed by the late-time tail of the capture process.
figures_summary: Figures show non-monotonic dependence of $T_c$ on $\alpha$ and plateauing behavior with increasing $R$. Figure 3 compares near-optimal completion times for different assignment policies.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the model dynamics, analyzes the effect of walker persistence ($\alpha$) on $T_c$, and then systematically compares three distinct assignment policies (single-round, cascading, max-cardinality matching) to quantify their impact on the extreme capture time.
why_interesting: While not directly quantum, the study models complex non-equilibrium dynamics involving resource competition and state transitions, which shares conceptual parallels with modeling energy landscapes or information flow in open quantum systems.

Figure 3 shows that at R ≤5, the baseline and cas- cading policies agree within uncertainty. From R ≈10 onward, cascading reassignment becomes significantly faster, reducing Tc to roughly one third of the baseline value by R = 20–30. This effect persists when each policy is evaluated at its own optimal α and across larger lat- tices.
